items.title: e-infra
items.text: The python infra blueprint of the e-stack template systems: uv · ruff · ty · tach · prek · pytest · zensical.

items.title: What this is
items.text: Every module a system materializes lives once here — this is the infra blueprint the e-taxis wizard reads when it exports a new project, offering the user the parts that are optional. Services do not depend on this package at runtime: make infra in any system copies the sections of src/e_infra/ into its own src/ (byte-identical except import paths), so each system ships self-contained and this stays the single source of truth. make infra-check fails the moment a copy drifts.

items.title: Modules
items.text: All sources live under src/e_infra/, layered by tach — high to low: processors -> adapters -> infra -> ops. The purpose of each module is its first docstring line, verbatim; reference pages are generated from the sources: drop a new module under src/ and it appears on the next build.

items.title: ops — the closed registry of categories
items.text:
A module in ops/ names a category — what kind of tool it is, never one particular use of it; file is the reference: everything that tells and reads what a file is. Functions are <category>_<scope>[_<detail>]; classes carry the category as surname. Something new joins an existing category; a new category is a decision, recorded, and only while the count stays at 20 or fewer. tests/unit/test_ops_contract.py enforces the three rules against this table.

hash and crypto never overlap: hash takes no key and no secret (it names things); crypto needs a key or entropy (it protects things).

Category Holds Never algorithm algorithms no domain owns: MinHash/LSH, statistics, numeric normalization anything with a key or a secret — that is crypto compose stack documents discovered and merged under the compose-go rules deployment; running services crypto everything that needs a key or entropy: keyed ids, bearer tokens, password hashing, JWS/JWE, signatures, AES-256-GCM hashing without a key — that is hash file what a file is: detection, import-based discovery over an installed package static code reading — that is registry; structured content — that is parser hash hashing without a key or a secret: content addresses, every id a project mints anything that needs a key or entropy — that is crypto image images drawn by rule: the house wordmarks and logos, deterministic SVG raster or photo editing; terminal widgets — that is tui lexical text read and rewritten by rule: name keys, secret redaction, language identification typed value extraction — that is pattern parser structured formats read into values: Markdown events, records across versions, the bearer header rewriting text — that is lexical pattern typed tokens in text, validated and normalized: dates, amounts, identifiers, URLs the meaning of words — that is lexical registry static code registry: symbols by path through ast, importing nothing import-based runtime discovery — that is file snap snapshot galleries: the visual drift gate over sets of widgets unit assertions tui agnostic terminal widgets: the masthead and its kin application screens; domain widgets wrappers measuring wrappers: scope a block, read what it cost (latency) retry or timeout policy; domain logic

Thirteen categories are claimed of the twenty allowed; a new one is a recorded decision while the limit holds.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
make install      # sync deps + git hooks
make check        # lint + type + arch + validate + test
make cov          # coverage gate (>=90%)
make docs         # serve docs at :8000

Editing rule: src/e_infra/ and the shared root files change here; systems re-materialize. make infra-check in any system fails when its copies drift.

items.title: Releasing
items.text: How this project is published, documented and kept alive. The system is semi-automated: every mechanical step runs from one dispatch or a make target; only the per-repo switches are set by hand, once.

items.title: Versions
items.text: The git tag is the version — uv-dynamic-versioning resolves it at build time from git describe. There is no version string anywhere in the tree to bump, and therefore no release commit: a release is a tag.

items.title: Cutting a release
items.text:
make release minor       # or: patch | major (default patch)

Equivalent to gh workflow run release.yml -f bump=minor. The workflow then:

  1. computes the next vX.Y.Z from the latest tag (first release → v0.1.0),
  2. pushes the tag and opens the GitHub release with generated notes,
  3. builds sdist + wheel from the tag and smoke-tests the wheel in a clean env,
  4. publishes — each job only if its gate is on (below).

Republish an existing tag verbatim (e.g. after fixing the release notes): dispatch release.yml with the tag input set.

items.title: Optional gates
items.text:
Every publishing surface is inert by default: CI quality, tests and the strict docs build always run; deployment and publication require explicitly declaring what this repo is. The single manifest of gates is .github/ci.vars.example; make ci-vars lists it, and tests/unit/test_ci_contract.py fails CI if a workflow uses an undocumented gate or a gate ships enabled.

Gate Enables One-time setup beyond the gate DOCS_DEPLOY Pages deploy from main Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub Actions PUBLISH_PYPI PyPI publish (OIDC, no token) PyPI → project → Trusted Publisher: owner/repo + workflow release.yml + environment pypi PUBLISH_IMAGE ghcr image :vX.Y.Z and :latest none — uses the workflow's own GITHUB_TOKEN 
gh variable set DOCS_DEPLOY --body true
gh variable set PUBLISH_PYPI --body true
gh variable set PUBLISH_IMAGE --body true

A library enables PUBLISH_PYPI; a service typically enables PUBLISH_IMAGE and DOCS_DEPLOY. Nothing else to configure — there are no long-lived secrets in the release path.

items.title: Maintenance loop
items.text:
• CI (ci.yml): ruff · ty · tach · validate-pyproject · zizmor · pytest × {ubuntu, macos, windows} with a ≥90% coverage gate · strict docs build on every PR (broken links fail).
  • Dependabot (.github/dependabot.yml): weekly grouped PRs for actions and pip — every bump passes the same gates.
  • Docs: reference pages are generated from the sources (mkdocstrings); never hand-write a table the code can derive. Where a project promises behaviour (a contract), model it like e-serde's STANDARDS: claims in code, a test executing every claim against live behaviour, pages generated from the contract.
  • Reproducibility: exclude-newer pins the dependency supply chain; actions are pinned by full commit SHA, verified against their tag.

items.title: First release checklist
items.text:
1. make init <name> done, repo pushed, CI green.
  2. Decide the gates; set the variables above; do the per-gate one-time setup.
  3. make release minor → tag v0.1.0, GitHub release, artifacts live.
  4. Verify: pip install <name> (PyPI gate) or docker pull ghcr.io/....

adapters/anytomd: anytomd bound to Python — one engine for every format, PDF and image descriptions folded in.

items.title: e_infra.adapters.awa
items.text:
adapters/awa: the durable background engine — awa, a Rust Postgres job queue, behind BackgroundPort.

awa's runtime is tokio and sqlx; its Python handlers run on the app's own event loop. The queue lives in a database of its own (QUEUE_DSN), apart from the service's data. connect builds the client off the loop (its constructor connects synchronously) within QUEUE_TIMEOUT, migrates awa's schema and this adapter's own background.progress table — awa clears a job's progress when it completes, so the latest snapshot of each job is kept there, upserted on every report — then opens the whole pool (QUEUE_POOL) at once: an awa pool that must grow while the server refuses it a connection (out of slots) stalls its runtime — no claim, no shutdown — until one frees, so a pool not granted whole within QUEUE_TIMEOUT is an outage now, never a stall later. Ids cross the port as strings; an outage (DatabaseError, a timeout) is a BackgroundError, and so is a call that outlasts QUEUE_TIMEOUT (a host that never answers would hold it for the driver's thirty seconds); anything else propagates. Once the database answers again awa reconnects by itself. A cancel lands in storage at once; a handler in flight learns it by polling is_cancelled every QUEUE_POLL, and its scope is cancelled where it awaits. close drains the workers for QUEUE_DRAIN, then releases the pool, all within QUEUE_DRAIN + QUEUE_TIMEOUT: past it, a BackgroundError.

items.title: e_infra.adapters.base
items.text:
adapters/base: the implementation base for external services — connect, close, ping, async-context bridge.

The contracts the core consumes are the Protocols in adapters.ports; this class is the shared implementation skeleton: the lifespan only ever talks to connect/close (through the async-context bridge), so any backend drops into the AsyncExitStack unchanged. ping is the cheapest real check that the provider answers — a query, a readiness route, a protocol ping, a trivial job — and raises PingError when it does not; every adapter must say how, there is no default. survey pings many at once (asyncio.gather, each under the same limit, so the whole takes the slowest one and one that hangs holds none of the rest) and answers one AdapterPing per adapter, never a raise: the lifespans log it at startup, GET /ready serves it.

items.title: e_infra.adapters.docling
items.text:
adapters/docling: document conversion on docling-serve — any source in, the DoclingDocument and its renderings out.

The service, not the library: docling's models (layout, TableFormer, OCR) live in their own container and process, so the app carries no torch. Conversions run as server tasks — submit, long-poll the status, fetch the result — because the synchronous endpoint is cut off by the server's wait limit, and a hundred-page filing outlives it. docling-serve answers a status poll at once (its wait is not held), so the client paces the polls itself. One wreq client per app, opened and closed by the lifespan.

A source is a URL (str, fetched by the server), raw bytes (sent inline, base64) or a local Path (read here, sent inline). The conversion options come from DoclingSettings; options overrides them per call, in docling-serve's own names. The whole conversion is bounded by DOCLING_DEADLINE, carried as each request's own timeout (what is left of it), never as a cancellation of a request in flight.

items.title: e_infra.adapters.otel
items.text:
adapters/otel: TelemetryPort over the official OpenTelemetry SDK, exported by OTLP over HTTP or gRPC.

A singleton like every adapter: one per app, opened by the lifespan, closed by it. It owns its own TracerProvider — never the process-global one: two apps, two tests, two providers, zero cross-talk. The exporter resolves once: an injected SpanExporter wins (tests read spans in memory), then OTEL_ENDPOINT batches to a collector over OTEL_PROTOCOL, and with neither the spans are still minted — their ids correlate logs and outputs, they just leave no process. Sampling is parent-based at OTEL_SAMPLE. Each span yields an OtelSpan (the SpanPort): attributes, events and status may be written until the block ends; a clean exit settles OK, a raise settles ERROR with the exception recorded. Spans nest through the SDK's contextvars, so a span opened inside another is its child across awaits.

items.title: e_infra.adapters.pgqueuer
items.text:
adapters/pgqueuer: the default durable background engine, PgQueuer on asyncpg, behind BackgroundPort.

PgQueuer has no queues, only entrypoints: each port queue is one entrypoint, the kind travels in the payload and picks the handler. A queue's slots is the entrypoint's concurrency_limit, counted in SQL over every worker of the database (fleet-wide, where awa's slots are per process): PgQueuer refuses a per-worker cap below twice its batch, so a slot of one is only expressible this way. A settled job leaves PgQueuer's queue table (its log keeps status, picks and tracebacks, never the payload), so this adapter keeps each job's kind, queue, args, attempts and latest snapshot in background.job, written in the enqueue's own transaction. Retries are the adapter's: a failed attempt with attempts left raises RetryRequested. Each queue runs one QueueManager on a connection of its own (LISTEN, dequeue, heartbeats); a manager that dies with its connection is restarted by a supervisor after RESTART — PgQueuer does not reconnect by itself. Client calls (enqueue, reads, cancel, progress) go through an asyncpg pool.

items.title: e_infra.infra.background
items.text:
infra/background: work that outlives the call that asked for it — one interface over a durable engine or memory.

A work is registered once by kind, on a queue, and submitted by kwargs: await background.submit("annotate", documents=(...), force=True) answers at once with the job, queued. The work receives those kwargs and a reporter: each snapshot it reports (plain builtins) becomes the job's progress, written at most every throttle seconds and always once more when the work ends. A work that returns completes its job; one that raises is retried until its attempts are spent; a cancel interrupts it where it awaits.

The engine is a BackgroundPort: a durable one (the awa adapter: Postgres, survives restarts, rescues crashed workers) or MemoryBackground (a task group in this process; nothing survives it). Background always holds the memory engine and prefers the durable one: an engine absent, unreachable on entry, or failing one enqueue sends the work to memory with a warning, never a crash. A durable engine reports an outage as BackgroundError; any other error is the caller's and propagates. Ids are strings, an engine's own, so a lookup asks memory first, then the durable.

After seal() (the lifespan chain's last act) the graph is strict: no writes anywhere, and a typo on read raises instead of silently growing a node. The seal freezes the graph's shape; each leaf (stores, engines, lists) keeps its ordinary Python life.

A State is also a full MutableMapping — dict-compatible wherever a host framework (litestar) expects one. Attribute names that collide with mapping methods (keys, items) are read via state["keys"].

items.title: e_infra.infra.struct
items.text:
infra/struct: msgspec models validated however they are born — decoded at the edge or built in code.

msgspec validates only while decoding (decode, convert): a Struct(...) built in code skips every constraint — Meta patterns, bounds, custom types. CheckedStruct closes that gap with one path, msgspec's own: a struct built outside a decode re-validates itself by converting its builtin form back into its type, so every constraint, nested field and error location (- at $.output) is msgspec's, never a hand-written duplicate — and the instance then holds the checked values, exactly as if decoded. Cross-field rules go in _check, which runs once per instance.

A complex type is a checked type: a subclass of a builtin (dict, list, tuple, str, int, float) that validates in its constructor and raises ValueError — with any third-party library it needs, and any derived state (a compiled validator) cached on itself. It decodes through CheckedStruct.dec_hook — built from its decoded form, so validated — and encodes through CheckedStruct.enc_hook back to that builtin (msgspec encodes dict/list/tuple subclasses alone, never str/int/float ones). A type msgspec does not know and that is no builtin subclass stays refused.

Decoding is trusted: inside CheckedStruct.trusted() the instance skips the round trip (msgspec just validated it); CheckedStruct.convert is that decode for values already parsed, hook and trust included. Forgetting the block costs one redundant validation, never a missed one.

items.title: e_infra.infra.settings.agent
items.text:
infra/settings/agent: the agnostic agent's edge — per-provider key and base, tier endpoints, retries, timeout.

Every provider the agent can reach has two optional settings, <provider>_api_key and <provider>_api_base, read under the provider's own standard variable names (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY or GOOGLE_API_KEY, OLLAMA_HOST, AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK...), the very names any-llm and the official SDKs use; where a provider declares none, the <PROVIDER>_API_KEY / <PROVIDER>_API_BASE convention stands. All default to None: there is no contract until a call names a provider, so a missing credential is caught by the agent at run time, never at boot. Providers that authenticate through their cloud's own chain (Vertex AI via ADC, SageMaker via AWS credentials) carry a base only. CUSTOM is any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Tiers (AGENT_HIGH / AGENT_MEDIUM / AGENT_LOW) are typed sub-settings, one TierSettings each, set field by field (AGENT_HIGH__PROVIDER=vllm, AGENT_HIGH__MODEL=qwen3.6-27b, AGENT_HIGH__API_BASE=...) or whole as JSON; a tier declared is validated at load — a provider outside the table or a missing model fails the boot, while a tier left unset fails only the call that asks for it. items.title: e_infra.ops.compose
items.text:
ops/compose: discover a stack tree and merge chosen fragments into one parameterized document.

StackCompose reads <root>/<category>/<service>/compose.yml and answers two things: a flat catalog of what is available (discover, optionally with the host-reference edges each service names) and the merged document (merge), built from the chosen names or from in-memory fragment mappings — the objects the stack machinery answers for a chosen service. Everything travels on plain e-serde mappings: anchors and << merge keys are resolved at load, so the engine only ever sees data. The merge follows compose-go rules — unique lists append and dedup, environment and networks unify as maps, mappings merge recursively, scalars take the last word — and then applies the policy: the declarable one held in SpecCompose (project name, port pattern, network name, volume root) and the two imposable laws of the house stack, never configurable: every service carries container_name and hostname equal to its name, and every relative or named volume binds under data/<service>/. Interpolated published ports (${WEB_PORT:-8080}) pass through untouched — they are already parameterized; validation of the result belongs to docker compose config at deploy time.

items.title: e_infra.ops.crypto
items.text:
ops/crypto: everything that needs a key or entropy — keyed ids, bearer tokens, password hashing, JWS/JWE, AEAD.

Signatures and tokens ride on joserfc over cryptography; hashing without a key is ops/hash, and the two never overlap. Agnostic: the engine reads its configuration through CryptoConfig (what infra/settings/crypto satisfies, or the CryptoKeys that generate_keys mints), and its errors are its own.

bcrypt is Rust-backed, argon2 the PHC winner; async only where hashing is intentionally slow, everything else is microseconds.

items.title: e_infra.ops.file
items.text:
ops/file: agnostic discovery over an installed package — modules, classes, functions.

The sweep is single-level and import-based: files of the package directory, subpackages excluded; discovery means importing, so a module that fails on import fails the sweep. Symbols are own only: re-exported names never count. A leading underscore is private at file level too: _helpers.py is imported never and seen never. discover dispatches on the target's type: a Kind sweeps a category, a base class selects its subclasses (never itself), a module reads that module alone, a predicate decides freely; pattern filters the resulting names. adiscover/asummaries offload the import walk to a thread.

items.title: e_infra.ops.image
items.text:
ops/image: deterministic square-font logos — banner by default, house colors, one rect per stroke.

Every wordmark is the same claim: a solid background and one group of rect glyphs in the house square font. The canvas is landscape by default — the banner hugs the word with a fixed margin, no dead square around a short name; landscape=False returns the reference 1024 square, where a word wider than the canvas scales as a whole. The font is the table GLYPHS: letters A-Z and the hyphen, each built from axis-aligned rects on a 255x436 box (stroke 45, pitch 292), anchored by the reference E reproduced byte-for-byte from assets/eager.svg. The geometry is uniform, never re-flowed, so the same name always emits the same bytes. Colors vary freely; the defaults capture the reference: background #060c15, letter #166b7e. A name that already carries the prefix passes through, filename spells the file the wordmark belongs to, and save writes it to disk.

items.title: e_infra.ops.registry
items.text:
ops/registry: static code registry — parse a scope with ast, register every symbol by its path, import nothing.

No module runs: facts come from ast.parse, the exact grammar of the running interpreter (3.14, PEP 695 included), so discovery has no import side effects and a syntax error fails the scan naming its file. The space is the model: nodes — packages, modules, files, classes, functions, methods, constants, aliases — carry a canonical dotted path (e_infra.ops.registry.CodeRegistry.snapshot) with a parent pointer; code keys are dotted inside the package prefix, raw files are keyed by their path relative to the root. The registry is a read-only Mapping, children answers one level down, and discover dispatches on the target's type: a Kind sweeps a category, a name selects the classes that syntactically name it in bases (never the MRO — nothing is imported), a predicate decides freely, pattern filters tails. Unlike ops.file nothing is hidden: _private.py and __slots__ are registered and flagged private. Only module- and class-level statements become symbols: a function body is opaque, its signature is the fact. snapshot pins the canonical bytes; ascan offloads the walk to a thread.

items.title: e_infra.ops.snap
items.text:
ops/snap: GallerySnap — the snapshot gallery for any set of Textual architectures.

Wraps pytest-textual-snapshot: register architecture names and viewports, get one clean test id per pair; the apps themselves arrive at run time through a fixture mapping (collection cannot import them). Usage, in a test module beside a conftest holding apps: dict[str, Callable[[], App]]:

_CASES = GallerySnap(("standard", "curves")).cases()

@pytest.mark.parametrize(("name", "size"), _CASES)
def test_gallery(snap_compare, apps, name, size):
    assert GallerySnap.shoot(snap_compare, apps, name, size)

Accepting a snapshot is a human act: --snapshot-update regenerates the SVGs under __snapshots__, review the diff, commit. The gate then fails on any visual drift. Materialized only into tui services (api and cli exclude this file at materialize time).

items.text:
ops/wrappers: agnostic measuring wrappers — scope a block, read what it cost.

Every wrapper is a context manager, sync and async alike (with works inside coroutines: the measure is the block, not the event loop). LatencyWrapper reads the monotonic nanosecond clock once on entry and once on exit; inside the block ms is the live elapsed time, after the block it is frozen — so a failure path can report how long it ran before raising.

items.title: e_infra.processors.doc
items.text:
processors/doc: the DocProcessor — every page read by the engine that reads it best, as fast as the pair allows.

Hybrid by measurement (10-K and paper corpus, 2026-10-13). liteparse (Rust, in-process) reads a whole filing in under a second and matches docling on running text — 98.7% of docling's words — but not on tables: rows fused or split on ~4 in 10 table pages, captions and formulas absent. docling-serve reads tables with TableFormer, crops and classifies pictures, OCRs scans keeping their tables, at ~1-1.7 s a page plus ~1.8 s a request. No signal liteparse computes before parsing predicts which of its tables are wrong; what it does tell, almost free, is which pages hold tables, figures or scans. So:

  1. liteparse reads every page (aparse, off the loop) and reports its signals per page;
  2. the pages whose signals are in DOC_ROUTE go to docling — the rest keep liteparse's reading;
  3. routed pages become spans: neighbours closer than DOC_GAP pages merge (a request costs more than the pages between); a long run halves into DOC_CONCURRENCY lanes when each half still pays off (LANE);
  4. each span asks docling only for what its pages need — OCR for scans, pictures for figures, TableFormer in DOC_TABLES mode — and spans convert concurrently, bounded; a failed span falls back to liteparse, said so.

The processor holds the document port (docling) and its own liteparse parser — singletons both — and no state per document: process returns a Document whose objects are engine-neutral.

items.text:
processors/md: the MDProcessor — any file to Markdown, detected and rendered by the anytomd engine.

Detection, every format's conversion, PDF reading and image description live behind one port (MdConvertPort, anytomd's binding); this processor only guards the size, unpacks a ZIP and re-enters each member in parallel, and records an engine's failure per file so one bad member never sinks a batch. It holds no state: convert is a pure function of bytes that returns a typed list of rendered files.

processors/models: what the processors hand out — a document read, or the Markdown a file becomes, both typed.

Interior data built by code: frozen, slotted dataclasses, never a boundary model. Whoever read a page (liteparse or docling, see Page.backend), its objects look the same: every one keeps its ref — the engine and its own pointer (docling:110-119#/tables/3, liteparse:p44/b7) — and the page it sits on, so anything extracted from it traces back to where it was read. Labels follow docling's vocabulary (section_header, text, list_item, formula, ...): liteparse blocks are mapped onto it.
